listeningParts.title: Hiring a stall at a neighbourhood market
listeningParts.contextDescription: A first-time seller telephones the organiser of a neighbourhood market.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Ashfield Neighbourhood Market, Ellen speaking. If you're ringing about this Sunday's event, the visitor entrance is beside the station. Stall bookings are handled here too, so let me know which information you need.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: It's about booking a stall, actually. I've been making bags from reused fabric, and a friend suggested trying your market. I've never sold at an event before, so I have quite a few questions. Would a new seller be allowed to join this month?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, provided there's space and the products fit our guidelines. Everything must be made, grown or repaired by the person selling it. We don't accept people buying ordinary goods in bulk and simply offering them again. Your bags sound appropriate. Would you bring anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: Probably some small purses, made from the pieces left over after I cut out the bags. I'd like to show people how I use the fabric, though I wouldn't be sewing there. Is there room to put a little display behind the table?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There is, but don't attach it to the wall. We have freestanding boards that you can borrow. The tables are inside the old school hall. Outside spaces are reserved for plant sellers because they need more room and sometimes bring wet pots. Everyone selling fabric items is indoors.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: That would suit me. A leaflet I picked up says a stall costs twenty-five pounds. Does that include a table, or do I have to bring one from home? I haven't got a suitable vehicle for carrying furniture.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That leaflet covers our larger summer event. For this monthly market, the fee is eighteen pounds, and that includes one table. Bring a cloth to cover it. We provide chairs, so you don't need to carry those. You can book a second table, but I suggest starting with one.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: Yes, one should be enough. What time should I arrive? I saw that the market opens at ten, so I thought perhaps half past nine would give me enough time to arrange everything without being too early.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Please arrive by nine instead. Vehicles have to leave the courtyard by nine thirty, and we need time to check the walkways before the public enters. You can unload in the courtyard, then park at the library. Market sellers can use its car park free on Sundays.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: Right, nine o'clock. And can I use an electronic payment machine? Mine usually connects through my phone, but the signal isn't always reliable in older buildings. I don't want to arrive and discover I can only take cash.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: There is wireless internet, and we'll give you the password on arrival. We can't guarantee that every payment device will work, so bring a cash float as well. We don't exchange money at the information desk. Also, there's no electricity at individual tables, unless you've booked a demonstration space in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Could you take my details now? My name's Louise Fenwick. That's F-E-N-W-I-C-K. The business name is Patchwork Lane, although I haven't printed any signs yet.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Thank you. Please email a photograph of your products, so we can confirm they meet the guidelines. We don't need a photograph of your workspace. Once we've approved the products, we'll send a booking form. The deadline for returning it is Thursday, not Friday as it was last month.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: I'll send that tonight. Will I be told which table I've got before the day? I'd like to work out how to arrange the bags, particularly if the table is close to a doorway.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Your confirmation will include a table number. We keep all entrances clear, and there will be a plan at reception. One last thing: packaging. Please avoid plastic carrier bags. Paper is acceptable, but we encourage customers to bring their own bags. You're welcome to put up a small notice explaining that.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: That fits well with what I'm making. Thank you for explaining everything. I'll wait for approval before printing the table number on anything, and I'll make sure the cloth and cash float are packed the night before.

listeningParts.title: A welcome to the riverside walking festival
listeningParts.contextDescription: A volunteer coordinator explains the programme and arrangements for a local walking festival.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Welcome to the riverside walking festival. Before you choose a walk, I'd like to explain a few changes to the printed programme and how our activities work. The festival is intended for local people as much as visitors, and none of the walks requires specialist knowledge. We hope you'll notice something unfamiliar even on a street you use every day.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Our first route, the Doorway Walk, looks at how buildings meet the street. You won't go inside private homes. Instead, the guide will ask you to notice entrances, steps, gates and the small spaces where neighbours sometimes stop to talk. It is a short route with frequent pauses, so it suits people who enjoy discussion rather than covering a long distance. It finishes where it begins, at the clock tower.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The Waterline Walk follows the river path. It was advertised as a complete circuit, but repairs to the footbridge mean we must return along the same bank. The total distance is unchanged. This route is mainly about the working river: loading places, old workshop entrances and the ways different activities have occupied the bank. It isn't a wildlife identification walk, though you may certainly see birds.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The third route is called Listening to the Street. For part of it, the guide will ask everyone to stop talking and pay attention to the sounds around them. You don't need to record anything. In fact, we'd prefer phones to remain in pockets during those short periods. Afterwards, there will be time to compare what people noticed. Someone near the front may have heard a different sound from someone at the back, which is part of the interest.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Finally, the Sketching Walk is not an art class. You don't have to produce an attractive picture, and nobody will assess your drawing. Making a quick sketch is simply a way of looking carefully. The guide may ask you to mark where people sit or how they move through a square. We can lend pencils, but bring your own notebook. Loose sheets tend to blow away when we're near the river.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: All four walks are free, but places are limited because large groups can block narrow pavements. Collect a coloured ticket at the registration desk for the route you want. Please take only one ticket per person. If you later change your mind, return it so someone else can use the place. Booking a place on a walk does not reserve a seat at the evening discussion; that has a separate ticket.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: A few practical matters now. The printed map shows toilets inside the sports centre, but that building is closed today. Please use the public toilets behind the theatre. Drinking water is available here in the courtyard, so fill your bottle before leaving. There are no refreshments included on the routes. Some pass cafés, but the guides won't make a scheduled stop for buying food.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: If heavy rain makes a route unsuitable, we will hold its discussion in the gallery rather than cancel the entire session. You can look at photographs and talk about what the walk was intended to explore. This alternative obviously doesn't replace being outside, but it still gives you a chance to exchange observations. Check the noticeboard before your start time, as that is where any change will be posted.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Please respect the people who live and work along the routes. Avoid photographing someone at close range without asking, and keep doorways clear when the group stops. Our guides are volunteers, and they have been asked to prioritise safe movement over finishing every planned stop. If the group is moving slowly, some material may be discussed back here afterwards. Enjoy your walk, and bring your questions to the discussion when you return.

listeningParts.title: Choosing an observation site for a planning assignment
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two students discuss how to investigate the use of a small public square.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: I've been looking at possible squares for our planning assignment. The large one outside the station would be interesting, but it would be difficult to observe all the entrances at once. I think Mill Square is more manageable. We could see the whole area from the low wall beside the café without standing in anyone's way.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: I agree about the size, but wouldn't sitting beside the café influence what we notice? We might focus on customers using its tables and miss people just crossing the square. We should draw the boundaries of the area before we start, so we're both recording the same space.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Good point. Let's include the paved square but exclude the café's private seating. We can still note whether people move between the two, but we shouldn't count a café customer as using public seating. The surface makes that boundary fairly clear: the café has timber decking, while the square is paved.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: Our question was whether the square provides places to rest. At first I thought we could count occupied benches and use that to judge demand. But someone might sit on the wall because all the benches are full, or because they prefer the view from there. So counting benches alone would miss other forms of sitting.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Then let's record the location of each seated person, not just whether a bench is occupied. We can mark locations on a plan. We should avoid guessing ages, though. We'd have no reliable basis for saying a particular person is sixty rather than fifty. We can discuss access needs without assigning everyone to an age group.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: What about people who stand still? They might be resting too, but we can't tell from a brief observation. I suggest we record standing separately and explain that the category describes a visible position, not a person's intention. That would be more accurate than calling everyone who stops a resting visitor.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Yes. And we need a rule for recording movement. If somebody walks across, leaves and then returns, we can't necessarily recognise them. Let's count crossings as events rather than claiming to count unique individuals. That means our report must say crossings, not visitors. The distinction sounds small but changes what the total means.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: For timing, I can manage Tuesday morning and Wednesday afternoon. Those are the only periods when neither of us has a class. We'd originally considered Friday evening, but there's a temporary food market then. That would make the square quite different from its normal arrangement.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We should actually mention the market as a limitation. Two daytime sessions won't tell us how well the space works during events. We don't have to pretend our sample covers every use. Maybe the report could end with questions for a later study rather than a complete redesign of the square.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: Before the main sessions, could we do a ten-minute trial together? We might find that the categories overlap or that the plan is too small to mark clearly. I'd rather discover that now than after collecting two hours of notes we can't compare.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Definitely. We'll each make independent records during the trial, then compare them. If our descriptions differ, we'll refine the definitions. We should also record the weather, because it may affect whether people choose exposed seats. We can't isolate its effect from two visits, but readers should know the conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Jonah
dialogue.text: And no photographs of individual people. A sketch of the empty layout should be enough for the report. If we want opinions, we can propose interviews as future work instead of approaching people without having prepared a clear consent process. For this assignment, careful observation is already a substantial task.

listeningParts.title: Describing a neighbourhood through routes
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecturer introduces the use of route descriptions in urban observation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A neighbourhood can be described as a collection of buildings, but it can also be understood through the routes people use. A route connects activities in a sequence: leaving home, taking a child to school, buying food and reaching a workplace. Looking at that sequence helps us see why a small obstacle can matter much more than it appears to on a map. Today's lecture considers what route descriptions can reveal, and where their limitations lie.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Begin by distinguishing distance from effort. Two routes of equal length may involve different demands. One could include steps, difficult crossings or an exposed stretch without shelter. Another might be longer on paper but easier for a person carrying shopping. A route description should therefore include obstacles, not merely the total distance. It should also avoid assuming that every traveller has the same physical capacity, equipment or reason for being there.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next issue is time. A crossing that causes little difficulty at midday may be uncomfortable during the school run. A passage that is available during business hours may be locked in the evening. Record when an observation was made, and distinguish a permanent feature from a temporary condition. A parked delivery vehicle can block a path, but a single encounter does not establish that the path is always blocked. Repeated observations or other information would be needed for that conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Routes also involve decisions. At a junction, a person may choose the familiar way even if a sign suggests a shorter alternative. An observer can record which direction was taken, but should not infer the person's reason from movement alone. If reasons matter to the project, an interview may be appropriate. Its questions should allow people to describe their own priorities rather than invite agreement with the planner's preferred explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A useful recording method combines a simple map with a narrative. The map shows where something happened; the narrative explains the sequence and the conditions. Either on its own can lose important information. A map covered in symbols may be difficult to interpret without a key, while a written account may leave the reader uncertain about the location. The two should refer to each other clearly, using consistent names for the same places.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Be cautious when comparing accounts. Someone who walks the route daily may describe a confusing turn as obvious because they no longer need to think about it. A newcomer may notice the missing sign immediately. Neither account should simply replace the other. Their difference can reveal how familiarity affects the experience. The planner's task is to understand that difference, not to decide that the experienced person must provide the correct description of everyone's journey.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A route study can generate possible improvements, but these proposals need checking. Removing a barrier in one place might change deliveries or access somewhere else. Before recommending a permanent alteration, consider who uses the space for purposes not included in the initial account. This is particularly important when the person who supplied the account is only one of several groups affected. Listening carefully to one experience should expand the enquiry rather than close it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, explain the scope of the work. A detailed account of one journey is valuable as an account of that journey. It does not automatically represent every resident. State which routes were examined, under what conditions and whose experiences remain absent. Then the reader can use the account appropriately. Even a photograph of an open gate should be accompanied by information about when access was checked, rather than being offered as proof that the route is permanently available. Route descriptions become most useful when they connect the physical arrangement of a place with the practical activities that people are trying to carry out.

groups.instruction: Questions 31–40. Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

readingPassages.title: The routes between places
paragraphs: A map can show two destinations close together while revealing little about the journey between them. The straight line connecting a home and a shop is a geometric relationship, not necessarily a usable route. A fence, a missing crossing or a change in level may require a substantial detour. To understand access, therefore, it is necessary to consider the network of available connections rather than simply the positions of destinations. This distinction is especially important when a plan appears to provide a facility nearby but leaves the practical route to it unresolved.

Imagine a neighbourhood with a school on the opposite side of a busy road from its housing. Measuring the distance from each front door to the school gate would not establish how easy the journey is. The location of a suitable crossing matters, as does the route through the school grounds. A gate that is physically close but kept locked cannot be treated as an entrance available to pupils. A useful description must distinguish what can be seen on a drawing from what people are actually permitted and able to use at the relevant time.

Distance is not the only cost of travelling. A path with frequent obstacles may require more attention or effort than a longer unobstructed alternative. Consider someone pushing a loaded trolley. A short flight of steps could make the direct route impractical, even though a person walking without equipment might scarcely notice it. The point is not that one route is universally better. It is that a comparison needs an explicit account of the user and the task. Without that account, the phrase 'most convenient route' can conceal rather than resolve a disagreement.

Connections may also change over a day. A passage through a shopping building might shorten a walk while the shops are open but become unavailable after closing. An observation made during the afternoon would not reveal this limitation unless opening arrangements were checked separately. Temporary conditions matter as well: a delivery can occupy a narrow path for a short period. These examples call for careful descriptions of when a route was examined. They do not justify assuming that a single obstruction is permanent or that an apparently clear route will always remain clear.

The attractiveness of a route can influence its use without changing its physical length. Shelter, places to pause and opportunities to see other people may be relevant to a walker. However, these preferences should not simply be assigned to users by an observer. A person might choose a shaded street because it is familiar, because a friend lives there or for a reason unrelated to shade. Observing the chosen route establishes a movement, not its motivation. If the reason is central to an investigation, the person may need to be asked directly.

A route description can combine several kinds of record. A plan locates a crossing or barrier; a written account describes what happened there; a note of the time supplies context. Linking these records makes an account easier to interpret than presenting them separately. Consistent labels are important. If one record calls a place the south gate and another calls it the garden entrance, a reader may assume that two different locations are involved. Clear naming is a modest task, but it can determine whether someone else can follow the observation at all.

Changes to a connection need to be considered beyond the immediate inconvenience they address. Opening a gate could help pedestrians while creating new responsibilities for the people maintaining the site. Moving a crossing might benefit one route and lengthen another. These possibilities are not arguments against improvement. They are reasons to identify the groups affected and examine the proposed arrangement as part of a network. An intervention at one point can alter the practical choices available elsewhere, so its value cannot always be judged by looking only at the original obstacle.

A careful access study is consequently more than a search for the shortest line. It describes connections, permissions, conditions and the activities people need to carry out. Even a small study can be useful if its scope is clear. An account of a journey with a trolley need not claim to represent every journey in the neighbourhood. It can identify a particular difficulty, explain how it was observed and suggest what further information would help. Understanding access begins with destinations, but it becomes practical only when the routes between them are taken seriously.

readingPassages.title: A timetable as a model
paragraphs: A timetable appears to be a list of departures and arrivals, yet it is also a model of how a transport service is expected to work. It connects journeys, vehicles, stopping places and the time needed to move between them. The printed page shows only selected results of those relationships. A passenger may reasonably care most about one departure, while an operator must consider whether the same vehicle can complete an earlier journey in time to begin it. Reading the page as a set of independent promises can therefore hide the connections on which those promises depend.

One basic distinction is between travel time and the interval between services. A bus may take twenty minutes to reach its destination, while departures from the starting point occur every fifteen minutes. These figures answer different questions. The first concerns a journey; the second concerns how frequently an opportunity to start that journey is offered. Neither tells a passenger how long they will actually wait without further information about when they arrive at the stop. Even simple numbers need an explanation of what is being measured before they can support a practical decision.

Connections introduce another layer. Imagine two routes that meet at an interchange. If an arriving service is scheduled to reach it one minute before the other departs, the paper connection may look efficient. In practice, passengers could need time to leave one vehicle, find the right platform and board the next. A connection is not just a relationship between two clock readings. It is an activity carried out by people in a particular place. Its adequacy depends partly on the layout and on the needs of those expected to transfer.

A schedule also has to accommodate variation. Traffic, boarding and other circumstances can affect how long a journey takes. Adding spare time can reduce the chance of a small delay spreading, but that time has consequences. Passengers already on board may experience it as an unnecessarily long pause if the vehicle arrives early. The planning question is not whether every pause is wasteful or every buffer is desirable. It is where an allowance serves a clear purpose and how its effect is balanced against the time experienced by users.

Comparisons between published and observed journeys require care. A service that reaches its final stop on time may still have left an intermediate stop early, inconveniencing a passenger who arrived according to the timetable. Conversely, an average delay at the terminus may conceal substantial differences between individual trips. A useful evaluation identifies which event was measured and describes the distribution of results when that matters. One headline figure cannot establish that every passenger encountered the same conditions or that all stages of the journey performed equally well.

Information design affects whether the model can be used. A timetable may distinguish weekdays from weekends through a small symbol whose meaning appears elsewhere on the page. An experienced passenger may interpret it instantly; an unfamiliar user may not notice it. Testing should therefore involve an actual task, such as finding a possible departure on a specified day. Asking whether the page looks clear is a weaker test of practical understanding. It is possible to approve the appearance of a timetable and still choose a service that does not run on the required day.

Changes require coordination across the places where information is available. A revised departure may appear on a website while an older version remains at a stop. The contradiction creates a problem that cannot be solved merely by making each version attractive. Somebody must identify the affected records, update them and make the current arrangement clear. Temporary changes need particular attention because they can outlast the notice intended to explain them. A useful information system records when an alteration begins, when it is expected to end and who will check whether the original schedule has resumed.

The timetable is therefore best understood as a public account of a planned system, rather than a complete description of every journey that will occur. Its usefulness depends on operational assumptions, sensible allowances and information people can interpret. This does not make precise departure times meaningless. It explains why precision on the page must be supported by a process behind it. When evaluating a timetable, the appropriate question is not simply whether the numbers are neatly arranged, but whether the relationships they express provide a credible and usable plan for travel.

readingPassages.title: Who decides what a public square is for?
paragraphs: A public square may be described as an open space for everyone, but that description does not resolve how it should be used. One person wants somewhere quiet to sit, another hopes to organise a market, and a third needs a direct route between streets. These uses can coexist at some times and compete at others. In my view, the purpose of planning is not to discover one activity that defines the square forever. It is to make a reasonable arrangement between uses while recognising that the people affected do not all have equal opportunities to express their preferences.

The visible popularity of an event is relevant, but it is not a complete measure of public value. Imagine a square filled with visitors during a weekend market. The crowd demonstrates that the event attracts people who can and wish to attend. It does not show what happened to someone who normally rests there, or whether a person avoiding crowds stayed away. I would resist the claim that the busiest arrangement must be the best one. Absence is harder to observe than attendance, yet it may still reveal a consequence worth investigating.

This does not mean that temporary events should be excluded. A market or performance can introduce people to a place and support forms of social contact that do not occur during an ordinary day. The problem arises when a temporary use gradually becomes the default without a clear decision about what it replaces. If setup, the event itself and clearing away occupy most of a weekend, describing the activity as lasting only a few hours understates its effect. An honest account includes the surrounding work as well as the advertised performance or trading period.

Consultation can improve decisions, provided it is more than an invitation to endorse a finished proposal. Asking residents to choose between two complete layouts may leave the underlying priorities unexamined. It can be more useful to ask what people need to do in the space and what difficulties they currently face. I believe such questions should precede the detailed drawing. A preferred solution can then be evaluated against stated needs, rather than defended because considerable effort has already been invested in producing an attractive image of it.

Nor should consultation be treated as a simple vote in which the largest group automatically receives everything it wants. A requirement for a continuous accessible path is not equivalent to a preference for one colour of paving. Some needs concern whether a person can use the place at all. Others concern how enjoyable a particular use might be. Both deserve attention, but they may justify different levels of priority. In my view, explaining these distinctions is part of fair planning, even when it does not produce an outcome that pleases every participant.

A temporary trial can provide useful evidence. Movable seats or a limited event schedule may reveal practical effects before permanent work begins. But a trial is not automatically representative. The weather, publicity and novelty may affect who attends and how they behave. An evaluation should therefore explain the conditions and identify what remains uncertain. It should also give people a way to report difficulties. Counting those who used the trial arrangement, without considering people who could not use it, repeats the same limitation as judging a market entirely by its crowd.

Maintenance belongs in the decision too. A proposal that depends on moving furniture every morning requires someone with the time, resources and authority to do that work. If this support is absent, the intended flexibility may exist only in the plan. I would rather see an achievable arrangement than an elaborate promise that cannot be maintained. This is not an argument for permanent simplicity regardless of need. It is a demand that the practical responsibilities of an arrangement be considered alongside the experience it is intended to create.

Public squares cannot avoid choices about priorities. The reasonable aim is to make those choices explicit, test assumptions where possible and remain open to revision. Different uses may need different times, different areas or limits that protect access for others. In my view, success is not demonstrated by a photograph of a busy square on its best day. It is demonstrated by an arrangement that people can understand, that includes important needs and that has a credible way to respond when its effects differ from what was expected.
